title: Swelling behind the knee: is it a Baker's cyst, and does it need treatment?
seoTitle: Baker's Cyst: Swelling Behind the Knee Explained
metaDescription: A soft lump behind the knee is often a Baker's cyst. Learn why it forms, how it is checked, when it could be a clot, and why most need no operation.
intro: Many people notice a soft, tight swelling behind the knee, usually when they straighten the leg or after a long day of walking. It is natural to worry that it is a tumour or something serious. Most of the time it is a Baker's cyst, a harmless pocket of joint fluid. The one thing that should not be missed is a blood clot, so this article also explains the warning signs.
summary: A Baker's cyst is a fluid-filled lump at the back of the knee. In adults it usually forms because something inside the knee, such as arthritis or a meniscus tear, is producing extra fluid. It is benign, is confirmed with an ultrasound, and usually settles when the underlying knee problem is treated. Surgery to remove the cyst is rarely needed.

sections.heading: What is a Baker's cyst and why does it form?
sections.body:
A Baker's cyst (also called a popliteal cyst) is a fluid-filled lump at the back of the knee. In adults it is usually a sign of another knee problem, such as osteoarthritis, a meniscus tear, an old injury, rheumatoid arthritis or gout, that makes the joint produce extra fluid, which collects in a pouch behind the knee. The NHS notes it is more common in people aged 35 to 70.

Think of it as a side effect rather than a separate disease. A review in Sports Health (Frush and Noyes, 2015) reported that these cysts are found together with a problem inside the knee in up to 94% of cases, with meniscus tears the most common partner. In children, there is often no clear cause and the cyst tends to go away on its own.

sections.heading: What symptoms does it cause?
sections.body:
Many Baker's cysts cause nothing more than a lump you can feel behind the knee. Others cause a feeling of tightness or fullness, aching, stiffness, difficulty bending the knee fully, or clicking. Symptoms are often worse after walking or standing for long periods, and the lump may look larger when the leg is straight.

Because the cyst usually reflects what is happening inside the knee, you may also have the symptoms of that underlying problem, such as pain on the inner side of the knee with a meniscus tear, or morning stiffness and pain on climbing stairs with arthritis.

sections.heading: Could it be a blood clot instead?
sections.body:
Yes, and this is the most important thing to rule out. A deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a blood clot in a leg vein and can also cause calf pain and swelling. A Baker's cyst that bursts can leak fluid into the calf and look very similar. You cannot reliably tell them apart at home, so new calf swelling needs prompt assessment.

The NHS advises getting urgent medical help if leg pain or swelling suddenly worsens, or if you notice bruising, warm skin, red or darkened skin, or swelling that becomes firmer or softer. If leg swelling comes with breathlessness or chest pain, treat it as an emergency: go to the nearest emergency department or call an ambulance, and do not drive yourself, because a clot may have travelled to the lungs. StatPearls stresses that a burst or very large cyst must be distinguished from a true DVT.

sections.heading: How is a Baker's cyst diagnosed?
sections.body: A doctor usually suspects a Baker's cyst from examining the back of the knee, then confirms it with an ultrasound scan. Ultrasound shows whether the lump is filled with fluid and, when needed, the veins can be scanned at the same time to check for a clot. An X-ray or MRI may be added to look at the cause inside the knee. The Sports Health review describes ultrasound as the usual first test, with MRI reserved for more detail, for example when the meniscus or cartilage needs assessing or surgery is being considered. An X-ray is useful if arthritis is suspected; see our guide on what a knee X-ray showing arthritis means.

sections.heading: Does a Baker's cyst need treatment?
sections.body:
Often not. A cyst that causes no trouble can simply be watched, and the NHS notes it may settle on its own, although this can take months or longer. When it does cause symptoms, the aim is to treat the knee problem behind it. StatPearls advises treating the underlying joint disorder in every patient with a symptomatic cyst.

In practice that usually means:
bullets: Rest from aggravating activity, an ice pack wrapped in a cloth for about 10 minutes at a time, and raising the leg
Simple painkillers, if they are safe for you
Physiotherapy to improve knee strength and movement
Treating arthritis or a meniscus tear in its own right

sections.heading: When are draining, injections or surgery used?
sections.body: These are second-line options. If the cyst stays painful despite treatment, a doctor may drain the fluid with a needle, often under ultrasound guidance, or give a steroid injection into the knee. Surgery to remove the cyst itself is rarely needed, because cysts tend to come back if the cause inside the knee is left untreated. The Sports Health review recommends non-surgical treatment for at least 6 weeks first, unless the cyst is pressing on nerves or blood vessels. It also notes that cutting out the cyst alone has disappointing results because of a high recurrence rate. When an operation is considered, it is usually keyhole surgery for the meniscus or joint problem, not cyst removal alone. See keyhole (arthroscopic) surgery.

sections.heading: What is the outlook?
sections.body: Good for most people. StatPearls describes the condition as benign with good outcomes in most patients. The cyst often shrinks or stops causing symptoms once the underlying knee problem is controlled, though it can come back, especially in older knees with arthritis. Recovery can be slow, so patience and keeping the knee active both help.

faqs.a: No. A Baker's cyst is a benign collection of joint fluid. An ultrasound can confirm it is a fluid-filled cyst and not a solid lump.

faqs.q: Will my Baker's cyst go away on its own?
faqs.a: It may. The NHS says cysts can improve without treatment, though this can take a few months to a few years. Treating the underlying knee problem gives it the best chance of settling.
Usually not as a first step. Draining or a steroid injection may be considered if the cyst stays painful despite treating the knee problem, but fluid can come back if the cause is not addressed.

faqs.q: How do I know if it is a clot and not a cyst?
faqs.a: You cannot tell reliably at home. Sudden calf pain or swelling, warmth, redness or bruising needs medical assessment the same day, usually with an ultrasound. Breathlessness or chest pain with leg swelling is an emergency.

faqs.q: Do I need surgery to remove a Baker's cyst?
faqs.a: Rarely. Removing the cyst alone often leads to it coming back. If surgery is needed, it is usually to treat the cause inside the knee, such as a meniscus tear.
